proposals.difficulty_range: Mid to very hard; the number of unbraked legs is the difficulty dial, and a two-baffle version with wide slots is approachable.
proposals.variant_axes: Slot alignment (near-vertical vs full-width zigzag); brake density; whether side walls are wall-jumpable or spiked so the redirect must come from a dash alone; adding one horizontal TimedHazard band that periodically seals a slot, so the fall must also be timed; a version with a 1-tile crawl slot at the bottom that requires arriving dash-compressed.

proposals.name: Banking Circuit (the loop with a ledger)
proposals.concept: A closed circular track around a central island, where the exit needs a coin count that cannot be gathered in one lap. Coins are scattered around the loop, but coins only bank when the player stands still or leaves the room, and the only standing-safe tiles are on the central island, reachable at two specific crossing points. So the room becomes: run a lap arc, collect, cross to the island, stand and bank, and go back out on a different arc for the coins you skipped. The twist is that the safe island is progressively contested — a TimedHazard covers half of it on a long period, so late laps must bank on the shrinking half, and the final coin sits on a spur that only connects back to the island via a dash the player must save.
proposals.why_novel: Loop layouts are only four rooms and none of them use the banking rule as a mechanic; the 18 dead-end coin vaults treat coins as a static payload behind one obstacle. This makes the banking rule itself the puzzle and gives the room a route-planning layer that no existing archetype has.
proposals.sketch: Central island: solid block x=12..19, rows 8..10, with a walkable top surface at row 7. Outer track: floor row 16-17 all the way across, ceiling ledge row 4-5 across, and both side walls climbable at x=1 and x=30 (clean tiles rows 5-15) so the lap is a real circuit — up the wall, along the ceiling ledge, down the far wall. Crossings to the island: a one-way platform bridge at (x=9..11, y=7) reachable from the west wall, and a 4-tile dash gap from x=24 to the island's east lip at x=20, y=7 (exactly at dash range, so the east crossing is boots-gated). Spikes on the outer floor at x=6..8 and x=22..25 (up-spikes row 17) make standing still on the lower track lethal, which enforces the island-as-bank rule. TimedHazard over island tiles x=16..19 row 7, period 200, active 100, so half the bank blinks. Final coin on a spur ledge at (x=26..27, y=11) with no floor beneath, so leaving it requires a saved dash back to the east crossing. Exit door east rows 13-16, gated on the full coin count.
proposals.difficulty_range: Early-mid for a plain two-arc version, late for the contested-bank version with a boots-gated crossing.
proposals.variant_axes: Number of crossings and whether they are one-way; whether the loop is horizontal (ring) or a figure-eight with a shared central corridor; how many coins exceed one lap's carry-safety; whether the hazard shrinks the bank over time or moves it; a variant where the island is the entrance and the loop must be run outward-and-back; a punishing variant where the only bank is a single tile.

proposals.name: Airlock Cascade (chambers that invert)
proposals.concept: Three or four small sealed chambers in a row, connected by narrow apertures, where each chamber restates the previous chamber's mechanic with one parameter inverted, and the aperture between them is a one-way commitment. Chamber 1: a squeeze under a low ceiling with a hazard above. Chamber 2: the same squeeze geometry rotated so the low gap is vertical and must be entered by a falling dash rather than a running one. Chamber 3: the geometry is identical to chamber 1 but the hazard is now a timed curtain instead of static spikes, so the same movement must now be scheduled rather than merely executed. The room teaches a motion and then re-asks it three times under changed conditions; the visible twist is that the player can see all chambers through the apertures from the entrance and recognises the shape of chamber 3 before reaching it.
core_verbs: re-execute a learned motion under a new constraint
proposals.why_novel: Crawl/squeeze is eight rooms and always exactly one beat — never developed, never varied, never combined. This class is the theme-and-variations treatment of it, and the chambered structure gives the multi-act narrative arc the lens asks for without reusing chimney or hop-corridor geometry.
proposals.sketch: Divide the room with two full-height solid walls at x=10 and x=21. Chamber 1 (x=1..9): floor row 17, ceiling slab at row 15 over x=4..8 leaving a 1-tile crawl channel at row 16 with down-spikes on the slab's underside at x=6..7 so an uncompressed player is killed; aperture through the x=10 wall at row 16 only. Chamber 2 (x=11..20): the aperture drops the player onto a ledge at y=13; a solid column pair leaves a 1-tile vertical slot at x=15, rows 9..13, entered from above, so the player must climb (wall strips at x=11 and x=20, clean, 4-tile spacing for jumps) to y=8 and then dash downward-through the slot compressed; spikes flank the slot mouth at (14,9) and (16,9). Chamber 3 (x=22..31): exactly chamber 1's slab-and-channel geometry mirrored, but the down-spikes are replaced by a TimedHazard filling rows 15-16 over x=25..29, period 100, active 50 — a 50-tick window, and a compressed crawl of 5 tiles fits in roughly that, so the act is a timed crawl with no slack. Exit east door rows 13-16 just past it. Coins one per chamber, banked at each aperture ledge where the player naturally stops.
proposals.difficulty_range: Mid; scales to hard by shortening the timed window in the final chamber or adding a fourth chamber that combines timing and vertical entry.
proposals.variant_axes: Which mechanic is the theme (squeeze, dash-length, wall-contact count, coin banking) — each gives a different room of the same class; number of chambers; whether the inversion axis is orientation, hazard type, or ability requirement; whether apertures are one-way or allow backtracking, which turns the room from a cascade into a comparison; a descending cascade where chambers stack vertically and apertures are floor slots.

ranked.name: Switchback Spine
notes: Soft positional failure is the single most valuable idea in the whole list: lets the top run be brutal without a checkpoint and gives the room a mental map. Demotion loop must be short or the re-walk becomes the filler it's replacing — keep the bottom run a 4-second sprint.

Soft positional failure — you fall two floors and walk it again instead of dying — is the single most first-timer-friendly idea in the whole set, and no existing archetype has it. Lets the top run be genuinely hard without unfair deaths. Only check: the fall path must actually be clear of the middle run's spikes so demotion never becomes death.

Soft positional failure is genuinely absent from the dungeon and costs nothing to implement. The build burden is alignment: top-run holes must line up with middle-run open sections for the demotion to reach row 16, which constrains all three floors at once. Also the middle crawl channel plus v-spikes at row 10 needs careful clearance checking.

ranked.name: Strata Sort
notes: Turns the flat drop-slot junction into an actual decision and stacks it five times. Recovery-by-jumping-back-up keeps experimentation cheap, which is right. Braided hole columns need care or one lane is obviously optimal.

Excellent newcomer property: 3-tile spacing under the 4-tile jump means a wrong lane costs time, not a life, so route choice can be explored rather than memorised. Real multi-route content built from the most under-used tile. Coin cluster forcing a stand-still bank on a spiked stratum is the one place the risk turns lethal — soften it.

Five one-way strata with braided holes is trivially buildable and the 3-tile spacing versus 40px jump correctly makes recovery possible-but-costly. Genuinely multi-route with a real risk/reward lane split. My favourite low-risk pick alongside Braided Crossing.

ranked.name: Shutter Chute
notes: Solid, but substantially Tide Shaft with fewer bands — pick one of the two as the class and make the other a variant. The one-shot-drop-vs-stage split is a good expert/cautious skill ladder.

Overlaps Tide Shaft heavily but is more forgiving: staging shelves mean the cautious two-stage solution always exists alongside the expert one-shot, which is exactly the difficulty gradient a first-timer needs. Bands are readable from a ledge before committing. Novelty docked for redundancy with the tide/band family.

Three full-width bands with staggered phases plus staging shelves — the two-stage/one-shot split gives skill expression for free. Only check: 6-tile horizontal shelf offset is 60px, described as 'drift plus one dash'; a 4-tile dash plus unquantified drift may not cover it. Make the offset 4 tiles or add an intermediate.

ranked.name: Low-Ceiling Arena
notes: Threat from above in an open room is a direction the dungeon has literally never faced, and the flow-state car-park feel is a real change of texture. Wells as the only vertical relief is a great structural payoff. Watch that a 3-tile band doesn't just feel like a corridor drawn wide.

Threat from above in an open space is the one axis every over-represented archetype ignores, and it is instantly legible — you can see the whole lid. Punishing the reflex jump is a teaching moment rather than a gotcha because the spikes are visible. Wells as the only vertical release give the room a clear shape.

Inverting the threat axis to the ceiling is the cheapest genuine novelty on the list — pure static tiles, no timing, no new primitive. A 3-tile playable band under a v-spike lid works against a 12px player, and the wells give legitimate vertical relief. Strong recommend.

ranked.name: Braided Crossing
notes: The foundational statement of multi-route, built from tiles that already exist. Slightly dutiful — one coin per lane to force two crossings is padding, not design. Ship it as the class that teaches the idea, then do better rooms.

The plainest, most legible statement of the two-route idea, built entirely from vocabulary the player already knows. Both lanes visible from the entry alcove is exactly right for a newcomer. 3-tile gaps 'barely clearable by running jump' is the one unfair edge — make the no-dash line comfortably clearable, not marginal.

The plainest statement of the missing multi-route idea and entirely static tiles — lowest build risk on the list. Numbers check out: 30px gaps under the 40px dash, 1-tile squeeze for compression, 5-tile spike spacing. Foundation class; ship first.

ranked.name: Tide Shaft
notes: Falling-as-metronome is the best idea here; stacked full-width TimedHazards with marching phase is legit engine vocabulary. Risk: fall speed vs phase step must be tuned or it's a coin flip, and full-width bands mean zero agency on some beats. Cut the floor spikes, they're filler.

Marching band of stacked TimedHazards is a genuinely new axis and reads well because the lit band is visible before you drop. Fair-death worry: a first-timer entering through the ceiling door arrives mid-cycle with no chance to read the pattern — needs a safe entry ledge where the tide is guaranteed off. Falling is fast, so a 24-tick band step may outpace player reaction; verify drop time between ledges empirically.

Stacked full-width TimedHazard rects with marching phases is exactly the under-used primitive and needs nothing new. Two engineering nits: 3-row ledge spacing is 30px, not the '~20px comfortable' claimed (fine as drops, marginal as recovery jumps), and the safe-pocket invariant only holds if active window 45 < phase step 24 is reconsidered — with active 45 and step 24, two adjacent bands are lit simultaneously for ~21 ticks, so the 'exactly one band lit' story is wrong. Retune to active<24 or accept a two-band front.

ranked.name: Metronome Gallery
notes: Honest reskin of the 19 hop corridors under a clock. Trivially buildable, teaches the timing language. But 'wait for the beat' with no execution demand is exactly the dead time a speedrunner hates — needs the against-the-player march variant to be worth a room.

The best teaching room in the set: first bay lets you watch two cycles, flat floor means no compound execution tax, deaths are legible ('I left late'). Deliberately re-skinning the most common archetype under a clock is exactly the right on-ramp for a first-timer. Slightly low novelty precisely because it is familiar, which here is a virtue.

Pure rect hazards on a flat floor; trivially expressible. Deliberate re-authoring of the most over-used archetype under a clock is a smart, cheap win. Phase step 19 vs active 34 again means overlapping lit curtains — check that the travelling gap is actually open; otherwise geometry is unimpeachable.

ranked.name: Metronome Bank
notes: Making rest the hazard is a genuine inversion and the rotating-shelf phase design is clean. The 1-tile expert perch as a hidden bank point is exactly the detail a runner will optimise toward. Small room, big idea.

'Rest is the hazard' is the sharpest one-line concept in the set and nothing in the dungeon does it. Rotating phases mean a safe shelf always exists, so it stays fair. Docked slightly because the 1-tile stepping-stone 'hidden hard bank point' is exactly the kind of pixel-precise secret that frustrates rather than rewards a newcomer.

Making the pause the skill check is the sharpest single inversion proposed, and three shelf rects at 120-degree phase offsets is trivial to author. The author correctly checks that an 8x12 player fits a 10px stepping stone. Only risk: active 100 of period 180 means shelves are unsafe most of the time and the rotation overlaps — retune duty cycle so a full safe rotation exists.

ranked.name: Forked Toll Crossing
notes: Differentiating routes by bank availability rather than difficulty is the sharpest anti-dominance trick proposed — that is what stops a fork collapsing. The double-pass return costing a full re-run of the dash is a great deterrent. Best of the fork family.

Differentiating the two lanes by bank availability rather than difficulty is the cleverest solution here to 'one lane collapses into the good one'. The decision changes with what you are carrying, which is real content. Upper lane's single 1-wide platform at dash's exact limit is the unfair part — widen it, or the top road is boots-plus-perfection.

Differentiating lanes by bank availability rather than difficulty is the insight that stops one lane dominating — the best argument for a fork in this batch. Build risk is the single one-way tile at col 16 row 8 reached by a dash of exactly 4 tiles: zero margin at the engine's stated limit. Widen to 2 tiles or shorten to 3.

ranked.name: Two-Clock Fork
notes: Arrival-dependent route cost is a genuinely smart way to stop one lane dominating. Boots-gating the high lane undermines that though — an ability gate turns a choice into a lookup. Make both lanes ability-neutral and let the clocks do the work.

Fills the zero-multi-route gap in the clearest way. Concern: 'coprime-feeling periods' means the cheaper lane changes per attempt, which reads as randomness to a newcomer rather than choice — start with the fixed-period variant. Boots-gating only the high lane is good honest signposting.

Best-argued multi-route case: branch-and-rejoin, both lanes solvable, arrival-dependent cost. Ability gate on the high lane (boots) is legitimate since the low lane is ungated. 'Wall-hug jump to a one-way platform' is vague; specify the step heights, and note 3-row rises are 30px, near the 40px ceiling.

ranked.name: Shutter Interchange
notes: Hazard-as-router is a real idea, but period 240 with a 60 window means a lot of standing around reading. A jaded runner will find the one lane that is always fastest and never look at the others. Halve the period.

Hazard-as-router hits the timed and multi-route gaps at once, and the long period (240) with short window makes it a reading puzzle rather than a reflex test, which suits a newcomer. The alcove you can watch a full period from is exactly the right teaching affordance. Coin inside rect A's footprint is fair because the off-window is long.

Hazard as routing mechanism is the strongest single idea here and needs only two rects. Antiphase guarantee (period 240, active 60, phases 0/120) genuinely leaves a route open at all times — the arithmetic holds. Ledge rises of 3 tiles are within jump. Very low risk.

ranked.name: Rotary Bank
notes: Hazard demands motion, economy demands stillness — cleanest thesis in the set. But four ring-sized rects plus notch dead-spots is fiddly geometry and the 3-tile notches must be exactly outside every rect or the room lies to the player. High payoff, highest authoring risk.

Lighthouse sweep plus stand-to-bank is a strong, original engine. Readability risk is real: four large hazard rects and a ring mean the lit side is often off-screen behind the central block, so the player cannot see the threat coming. Needs the banking notches visually distinct and ideally the sweep telegraphed.

Four side rects with 90-degree phase offsets is clean and the motion/stillness tension is a genuine new axis. Ring corridor 4 tiles wide inside 32x18 plus a 14x8 island fits. The 'notch outside every hazard rect' requires the rects to be authored around the notches — doable but check the listed left rect (50,20,40,140) does not overlap the bottom run.

ranked.name: Keyhole Vault
notes: Irreversible entry plus branching exit finally makes a vault a decision. Spike-throat one-way seal is clever and uses no new tiles. Verify the 8px body actually clips the side spikes on a wall-jump — the whole class rests on that hitbox claim.

Irreversible entry plus two priced exits is a real topology idea and rescues 18 stale vaults. Fairness hinges on the funnel being visibly one-way from above; if the player only learns it is sealed after falling in, it reads as a trap. Two exits at different ability prices does mean nobody is stranded, which is the saving grace.

One-way entry built from side-facing spikes against an 8px-wide body is clever and needs no new tile, but it is a hitbox bet: verify a wall-jump chain in a 2-tile throat actually clips the side spikes rather than threading them. Two exits with different ability profiles is a good answer to the 18 dead-end vaults.

ranked.name: Antiphase Airlock
notes: Structurally tidy and the deliberate opposite of Metronome Bank, but walking through floor-level doorways on a beat is the definition of filler for this persona — no execution tax, by its own admission. The unshuttered overhead lane is the only part worth keeping.

The most fair-death-friendly timed room proposed: gates are floor-level run-throughs with no execution tax, retreat is symmetric to advance, every chamber has a safe floor to stand and bank. A newcomer can go one chamber per cycle and never die while an expert rides one wave through. This is the room that should teach the whole timed vocabulary.

Cleanest build on the list: four partitions, four doorway-sized rects, strict 0/60 alternation at period 120 active 60, floor-level run-throughs so there is no execution tax. The unshuttered overhead lane that cannot bank is a well-judged second route. Nothing here needs measurement.

ranked.name: Shutter Crawl
notes: Compression-as-commitment is the right marriage of the two thinnest tags. Exit-shutter variant is the actual room. Watch that bay waits don't stack into dead seconds; three tunnels is the max before it drags.

Combines the two most under-used tags, but crawl-slide is uninterruptible, so a shutter that lights mid-tunnel is a death the player could not have avoided after commitment. Only fair if the entry shutter is the gate and the window provably covers full tunnel length plus margin. The proposal's own 'exit shutter, commit blind' variant should be banned for early rooms.

Combines the two most under-used tags and respects the key physics fact that crawl-slide is uninterruptible. Risk: a 6-7 tile tunnel is 60-70px against a 40px dash; the design leans on 'carried momentum' that may not exist. Verify slide distance empirically or shorten tunnels to 4 tiles.

ranked.name: Greed Loop
notes: Lap-length-as-wager self-balances without any hazard gimmick, which is rare and good. Risk is repetition: laps 2 and 3 over the same tiles is the exact samey-ness complaint unless coin depth changes the route shape, not just its length.

Push-your-luck lap length is a clean economic engine and the single bank tile at the entrance is readable and honest — you always know what abandoning costs. Coin 4 behind a 4-tile dash-cleared spike run is the outlier in difficulty and will be the thing that eats first-timers' whole laps; consider making it the optional last one.

Lap-length-as-wager is a real economic layer and everything is static tiles plus one-way stacks. Checks out dimensionally. Watch coin 3 ('upward-diagonal dash from row 5' to row 3) — that is 2 tiles up and within dash, fine — and make sure the single bank tile is genuinely the only spike-free stand, which requires auditing every surface.

ranked.name: One-Way Loop
notes: Directional asymmetry from one-way platforms alone is elegant and costs nothing. Ability-gating the ascent is defensible here because the room is a map object, not a crossing. Best 'learned as geometry' room in the batch.

Directional asymmetry via one-way platforms is a clean idea and true to the engine. But the spike placed at each descent platform's landing edge specifically to punish a re-climb is a trap that teaches by killing rather than by reading — a first-timer discovers the loop's one-wayness only via blood. Signal it with geometry, not spikes.

Directional asymmetry via one-way platforms is a real use of the engine's only directional tile. Weakness: the ascent side is a 4-tile-wide facing-walls wall-jump climb, i.e. literally the over-represented chimney, just short. Make the ascent a dash-up-diagonal or ledge puzzle to avoid re-importing archetype #1.

ranked.name: Shutter Ducts
notes: Peristaltic wave is a nice image and the dash-equals-one-zone-width tuning is disciplined to the point of unforgiving. Too close to Shutter Crawl to justify both as separate classes; make it that class's wave variant.

Peristaltic wave is a great image, but 'dash covers exactly one zone width with no margin for error' plus compression removing all escape options is the definition of an unfair death for a first-timer. Widen the pockets or shorten the zones. Coins inside hazard cells make the greedy line the unreadable line.

Peristaltic wave over a crawl corridor is a strong pairing, and the honest 'dash covers exactly one zone width, no margin' note shows the author checked the numbers. Concern: with period 120 / active 60 / step 30, two adjacent zones are lit at once for half the cycle — verify the wave leaves a coherent travelling gap. Pockets carved to row 12 give proper standing height.

ranked.name: Committed Fork
notes: Competent but it is Two-Clock Fork and Forked Toll Crossing wearing a third hat; three near-identical fork classes is its own kind of samey. The unbankable-in-flight coin ledger is the only distinct wrinkle — fold it into Forked Toll.

Fork visible from the entrance landing is exactly the information design a newcomer needs, and the within-route bank decision adds depth without adding execution. The irreversible one-way platform commitment is acceptable because both roads complete the crossing. Overlaps Two-Clock Fork and Forked Toll Crossing; pick two of the three.

Solid multi-route room with a within-route greed decision layered on the banking rule. Spacings (3-4 tile gaps, 2-tile rises, 1-tile squeeze, one 80/40 hazard) are all inside budget. The 'irreversible via one-way platform' commitment is honest since dropping through is the only transition. Low risk.

ranked.name: Airlock Cascade
notes: Theme-and-variations is the correct medicine for a dungeon that repeats shapes without developing them, and letting the player see chamber 3 in advance is excellent information design. Chamber 3's timed crawl with 'no slack' is a tuning cliff — give it a few ticks.

Theme-and-variations is the right cure for a dungeon that feels samey, and letting the player see chamber 3's familiar shape through the apertures before arriving is superb readability. Chamber 3's timed crawl with 'no slack' should be given slack. Also the strongest argument in the set for backtrackable apertures over one-way ones.

Chamber 2 requires the player to 'dash downward-through' a vertical slot, but dashes are horizontal or up-diagonal only — there is no down-dash, so that beat cannot be authored. Fix by making it a fall into a horizontal compressed entry. The theme-and-variations structure is the right treatment for the eight one-beat squeeze rooms and worth salvaging.

ranked.name: Catch Ladder
notes: 'The fall is easy, the stop is hard' is a sharp inversion, and cascading rather than killing mistakes is generous in the right way. The sketch's own numbers wobble (it corrects itself mid-sentence on offsets) — 8-tile gaps at 4-tile dash plus drift needs verifying.

Good inversion (the stop is hard, not the fall) and mistakes cascade rather than kill on upper tiers. But the sketch's own numbers wobble — 8-tile offsets between opposite nubs against a 4-tile dash plus drift is not clearly reachable, and 1-2 tile one-way landings after a multi-tile drop is a precision tax a newcomer will fail repeatedly. Verify the offsets before building.

Banking-under-pressure is a real new mechanic and one-way nubs cascading rather than killing is good design. But the sketch's own numbers wobble ('20-24 tiles... rather, 8 tiles'), and 8-tile (80px) offsets between opposite nubs are twice the dash. Halve the offsets or accept that every tier is glove-gated.

ranked.name: Phase-Offset Shutter Suite
notes: Best-structured act progression of the timed family: watch, commit, commit blind, ending dash-gated. The one-tile-apart antiphase pair with no standing solution is a genuinely nasty, memorable beat. Flat floor keeps it about time, which is the point.

Explicit watch/commit/commit-blind arc is good pedagogy and act 1 is a proper tutorial bay. But two curtains one tile apart in opposite phase with 'no standing solution' is a step change a first-timer will hit as a wall, and the author names the third act 'commit blind' approvingly. Front-load acts 1 and 2, park act 3 in a later room.

Act 2 as specified is broken: curtains one tile apart at phase 0 and 45 with period 90 / active 45 means one of the two is lethal at literally every tick, so the crossing demands a frame-perfect pass through the flip. That is not rhythm, it is a coin flip. Separate the pair by 3-4 tiles or shorten the duty cycle; the three-act teaching structure is otherwise excellent.

ranked.name: Duct Junction
notes: Crawling as the whole room rather than a beat, plus two structurally different solutions — hits both gaps at once. Constant compression risks a mushy, low-agency feel; the risers are what save it. Third merge duct is one branch too many.

Sustained crawl as the whole room, plus two structurally different solutions, is a big double fill. Readability is the risk: a solid-filled room carved into 1-tile ducts gives the player almost no sightlines, so the fork is chosen blind. The exit alcove where you can finally stand upright is a lovely release beat.

Sustained crawl plus two honest routes is the right target, but the risers are specified 1 tile wide with 'opposing solids so glove wall-jumps chain' — a 1-tile (10px) shaft around an 8px body leaves no room for a wall-jump arc. Widen risers to 3-4 tiles or replace them with one-way ledge stacks; otherwise the high lane is unreachable.

ranked.name: Commitment Slot
notes: Makes a coin detour an actual wager instead of a free back-out — the correct fix for 18 dead-end vaults. The hidden bypass duct is the good kind of speedrun secret. Verify the 3-tile-rise-through-1-tile-hole claim, the whole irreversibility rests on it.

Turning vaults into wagers is right, but it depends on the player judging a detour's cost before an irreversible slot, and the sketch admits the slot is one-way partly because arriving compressed through a 1-tile hole is awkward — that is a fuzzy physics claim, not a designed gate. First-timers will get pocketed. The visible bypass variant is the only version I would ship.

Turning vaults into wagers is the right fix for the 18 dead ends. But irreversibility is argued weakly: a 3-tile (30px) rise is inside the 40px jump, so the only thing stopping backtrack is needing to arrive compressed through a 1-tile hole. That is a hitbox bet, not geometry — test it, or deepen the drop to 5 tiles so the seal is unconditional.

ranked.name: Ratchet Descent
notes: Irreversibility plus an unbanked stack is the stakes descent has been missing, and 'is this the level I stop at' is a real recurring question. Overlaps Strata Sort structurally; differentiate by keeping this one strictly one-way.

Irreversibility plus a carried stack gives descent real stakes, and crucially most failures cost the coin route rather than a life — a fair pressure. The single mid-room bank shelf is a well-placed relief valve. Check the claim that a 3-tile gap is unclimbable while a 40px jump exists; that margin is thin and the whole ratchet rests on it.

The premise contradicts the stated physics: the sketch says 'between levels the vertical gap is 3 tiles: falling is free, climbing is impossible without gloves', but a 40px jump clears 3 tiles (30px) outright, so nothing ratchets. To make irreversibility real the tiers must be 5+ tiles apart, which does not fit five tiers in 18 rows. Rebuild with 3 tiers or accept it as a soft ratchet.

ranked.name: The Flue
notes: Pure commitment, zero filler, exactly the room a speedrunner replays. But it leans hard on air-drift authority and fall speed the spec doesn't pin down; 'about a tile per tick' is a guess. Prototype the physics before authoring baffles.

Vivid, but this is the least fair room here for a newcomer: instant death at fall speed, one-way commitment, and the whole column must be read before you drop even though you enter through the ceiling and cannot see the bottom. 'Failure is instant and legible' undersells the cost of a blind first attempt. Needs a pre-drop viewing ledge or much wider gaps.

The concept is legal tile-wise, but the physics claims are unsupported: 5-8 tiles of lateral travel per 3-tile drop relies on an air-drift speed the brief never states, and 'roughly a tile of drop per frame-tick band' is invented. Dash is 40px = 4 tiles, so the 7-8 tile offsets are strictly unreachable with one dash. Needs measurement before it is a class rather than a hypothesis.

ranked.name: Bank Run
notes: Hoard-and-cash-out because crawl posture cannot bank is the most mechanically inevitable idea in the list — the rule and the geometry imply each other. Ten-tile shafts of wall-jumping may drag; shorten the ring.

Hoard-then-cash is a genuinely fresh use of the banking rule and fills the loop gap. But ten tiles of 1-tile-wide shaft climbed by five wall-jumps is the spiked-chimney feeling under another name, and losing a seven-coin lap to one mistake is a punishment curve a new player will simply disengage from. Needs a cheap intermediate vault.

Same fatal detail as Duct Junction, worse: 1-tile-wide vertical shafts with '10 tiles of climb = about five wall-jumps'. Wall-jumping in a 10px-wide shaft is not plausible for an 8px body, and the whole ring depends on those two shafts. The hoard/cash-out economy is genuinely good — rebuild it around 4-tile shafts or one-way ledge stacks.

ranked.name: Needle Drop
notes: Dive-into-compression is a genuinely new compound move and the best expressive-movement idea after Switchback. But an 8-tile tunnel needing a mid-slide dash refresh may simply not be possible; spec doesn't say dash recharges without ground. Keep tunnels at 4.

Requires being dash-compressed at a specific mid-air height, then an 8-tile slide needing a mid-tunnel dash refresh — whether dash refreshes while compressed is unspecified and may not exist in this engine. Compound, unforgiving, and spikes on the approach lip punish the exact mistake a learner makes most. Build the 4-tile-tunnel easy variant first or not at all.

Chaining compression to descent is a good idea, but the flagship 8-tile tunnel needs a 'mid-tunnel dash refresh' — dashes normally recharge on ground contact, and whether a dash can even be re-issued while compressed is unstated. Four 2-tile slabs at rows 4,8,11,15 also leaves chutes of 2-3 tiles, tight for 'fall, turn and re-arm'. Buildable only in the 4-tile-tunnel variant.

ranked.name: Controlled Fall
notes: Great feel target, but the sketch requires 14-16 tile lateral moves per leg using wall-bounce redirects the engine may not support at fall speed, and one dash is only 4 tiles. As specified it does not work; it needs either far closer slots or physics that aren't in the vocabulary.

The three-act teaching structure is good but the geometry does not obviously work: slots 14-16 tiles apart require a fall plus a dash plus a bounce off a clean wall strip, chained at speed, and act 3 removes all brakes. That is a memorisation room. Better version of The Flue's idea, still the harsh end of the fair-death line.

Core traversal is unbuildable as specified: successive slots 14-16 tiles apart, explicitly 'far more than one 4-tile dash', resolved by an unspecified wall-bounce redirect mid-fall that the engine brief never promises. Also gates the whole room on gloves while calling itself the inverse of the chimney. Reduce offsets to 4-6 tiles and it becomes a good room.

ranked.name: Banking Circuit
notes: Route-planning layer is welcome but 'exit gated on a coin count' is a switch by another name and isn't in the stated vocabulary. Multi-lap forced backtracking is also exactly the repetition the player complained about. Fix the gate or cut.

Multi-lap ledger planning is genuinely new, but 'exit gated on coin count' is a lock-and-key mechanic nothing in the stated vocabulary supports — that is a new engine feature, not a level. Strip the gate and it becomes a good optional-greed loop. Shrinking-bank hazard on the island is the best part.

Fails on vocabulary: 'exit door gated on the full coin count' requires a lock/switch, and the brief states NO switches — doors are just gaps in walls. Strip the gate and the room still works as a lap-and-bank circuit, but the design's stated engine (must exceed one lap) evaporates. The blinking half-island is a nice touch worth keeping.

ranked.name: Well and Winch
notes: Good bones — cheap down, expensive up — but the sketch visibly flounders on door placement and mirrors itself into confusion. Overlaps One-Way Loop, which does asymmetry more cleanly. Merge or cut.

Strong idea (see your escape while you fall past it) but the sketch is visibly confused about door placement, mirroring and which wall the exit is on — it argues with itself mid-paragraph. Also overlaps Keyhole Vault and Greed Loop. Needs a clean re-spec before it can be judged as a layout.

Sound in outline, but the sketch visibly loses track of its own doors mid-sentence ('place exit on the left wall rows 4-7 ... so use the right-wall door with the room mirrored'), which signals the topology has not been worked out. Ascent ledges at 3-tile rise and 4-tile offset are legal. Needs a rewritten layout before it is authorable.
